title: Pathways to Information: Patterns of Language on Parade
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: In the fourth part of her series, Harriett Janetos argues that comprehension strategy instruction and knowledge building should be united rather than set against each other. Using her experience from kindergarten to AP English, she draws on Ehri, Willingham, Catherine Snow and Spencer and Petersen to claim that the patterns of language, including syntax and connectives, are what transfer across content. She pushes back on the claim that strategies only activate background knowledge, suggesting they also activate knowledge of language and text structure. Her conclusion is that strategy instruction needed rehabilitation, not burial, and that teaching language through knowledge-rich text is doable for typical teachers.
points: Instructional simultaneity teaches strategies, language and knowledge together to make the most of limited instructional time.
Sentence-level syntax and connectives are barriers to comprehension that knowledge alone does not remove.
Spencer and Petersen argue that teaching the patterns of language makes content come for free because language transfers across content.
Strategies do more than activate background knowledge; they build knowledge of how language and text structure work.
The knowledge-building movement should have repaired strategy instruction rather than dismissed it.
quotes: Like baseball, teaching is a game of failure—success interspersed with a fair amount of striking out. But like horseshoes, coming close to the target counts. If we can get our lessons to align with both reading science and learning science, the instructional changes—however incremental—can matter.

Comprehension strategies are meant to get students only to a rather basic understanding of a text. Reading strategies that hone other abilities, such as analyzing arguments and comparing points of view within the text, lead to deeper or more specialized understandings. And it’s my belief that learners likely benefit from greater practice in these reading activities.
If we actually teach the patterns of language—the content comes for free. And the patterns of language are what’s transportable across content.
The job has to be doable by the teachers we have—not the teachers we wish we had.

Content knowledge can’t be extracted from text unless students have both sufficient decoding skills and language comprehension skills, and the patterns of language are what’s transportable across content.
